planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Majesty is a female-flowered muscadine, so plant a self-fertile pollinizer such as Cowart or Nesbitt within 10-15 feet to ensure fruit set.

directions: Train onto a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Majesty was bred by Dr. Jiang Lu at Florida A&M University from a 'Supreme' x 'Triumph' cross and released in 2008, and it is notable for producing some of the largest berries of any released muscadine cultivar, with an attractive glossy black skin and excellent, sweet flavor. Because Majesty carries only female flowers it will not set fruit on its own, so a nearby self-fertile black or bronze muscadine is essential for pollination. Yields run lighter than the heaviest-cropping commercial cultivars, which is why Majesty is grown mainly by home gardeners chasing exceptional dessert-quality fruit rather than by growers prioritizing volume.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Muscadine Grape Breeding Program
Florida A&M University College of Agriculture and Food Sciences

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Polyanna is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer, ripening late (into October in zone 9) over a longer, uneven picking window.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a strong arbor or high-wire trellis. Polyanna was released by the University of Florida in 1998 from a 'Fry' x 'Southland' cross and stands out for its good resistance to fruit rot, a real advantage in the humid Gulf South where berry rot is a constant threat late in the season. The red-black berries are medium to large and self-fertile, so a single vine will set a full crop without a separate pollinizer. Because ripening is late and spread unevenly across the cluster, plan on picking over several weeks rather than in one pass, which actually extends the harvest season for a home vineyard.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Muscadine Grape Cultivars
American Pomological Society — Journal of the American Pomological Society

planting.note: Plant after last frost on a sturdy trellis in full sun; this is a dioecious vine, so a male Actinidia chinensis or compatible male kiwi vine must be planted within about 30 feet to set fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, training onto an overhead arbor or T-bar trellis strong enough to support a mature vine for decades. AU Golden Sunshine was patented by Auburn University from Chinese golden-kiwi breeding stock and selected specifically for its low winter-chill requirement and early fruit maturity, ripening about 20 days after fellow Auburn release AU Golden Dragon, making it far better suited to the mild winters of the Deep South than standard green-fleshed 'Hayward'. Fruit is cylindrical and smooth-skinned with sweet, non-acidic golden flesh, high soluble solids, and excellent flavor. Gold-fleshed kiwi types are generally more prone to bacterial canker (Psa) than green kiwi, so avoid overhead irrigation and prune to keep the canopy open for airflow.
sources: US Plant Patent PP22159 — Kiwi plant named 'AU Golden Sunshine', Auburn University
Auburn University College of Agriculture — kiwifruit research

planting.note: Plant after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Elmwood is a female cultivar needing about one male kiwi vine for every nine females, since kiwifruit is dioecious.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy arbor or trellis system. Elmwood is widely regarded as one of the best low-chill fuzzy kiwi selections available, needing only around 400-700 hours of winter chill compared to the much higher requirement of classic 'Hayward', which makes it a realistic choice for the mild winters of Gulf South gardens. Large, showy, fragrant white spring blossoms make the vine ornamental even before fruiting begins, and mature fruit is unusually large for a fuzzy kiwi, up to 10 ounces, with typical brown, hairy skin and green flesh. As with all kiwifruit, expect several years of vine establishment before the first meaningful harvest, and prune annually in the dormant season to keep fruiting wood productive and manageable.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Kiwifruit Production

planting.note: Plant after last frost on a strong trellis in full sun to part shade; Prolific is self-fertile (parthenocarpic) but yields improve with a male hardy kiwi such as Meader or Andrew planted nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade and train onto a sturdy trellis or pergola, since vines are vigorous twiners that live for decades. Prolific lives up to its name as a heavy, dependable bearer of smooth, grape-sized, edible-skinned fruit with a sweet flavor high in vitamin C, and unlike most hardy kiwi it can set fruit without a male pollinizer, though a nearby male still boosts yield. Like all Actinidia arguta it is far more cold-hardy than fuzzy kiwi, tolerating winter lows well below what would kill Actinidia deliciosa outright. Pick fruit while still slightly firm in late summer to fall and finish ripening at room temperature for the best flavor and to avoid losses to birds.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Actinidia arguta plant profile

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 grow in a large movable container so it can be sheltered from winter cold.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil, giving the epiphytic cactus a sturdy post or trellis to climb rather than the regular watering a typical fruit vine would need. David Bowie is a self-pollinating white-fleshed pitaya cultivar prized for its mildly sweet, distinctly lemony flavor, often described as a cross between kiwi and pear, wrapped in vivid pink-red skin edged with green triangular bracts. Flowers open only after dark and close by morning; because the vine is self-fertile, a single plant can set fruit, though hand-pollinating at night with a small brush improves fruit set in cool or humid weather. In zone 9, keep it in a container that can be moved under cover whenever frost threatens, since even brief cold exposure damages the succulent stems.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Hylocereus and Selenicereus varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dragon Fruit Production in Florida

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence after the last frost; Purple Giant tolerates brief dips to around freezing better than some purple passionfruit types but still needs winter protection in zone 9.

directions: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil. Purple Giant is valued for producing noticeably larger, rounder fruit than typical purple passionfruit, with heavy, rich pulp and a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor, self-pollinating readily on fragrant white-and-purple crowned flowers. Vines are fast to establish and often fruit within their first year from a rooted cutting, considerably quicker than seed-grown plants, and ripe fruit drops naturally from the vine at around 80 days from flowering. In zone 9, plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and mound mulch over the crown going into winter, since a hard freeze can kill purple passionfruit vines to the ground or outright.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Passion Fruit
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Passion Fruit Growing in the Home Garden

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun near a sturdy trellis or arbor; plant a second, genetically distinct Akebia nearby to improve the odds of the sausage-shaped edible fruit forming.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, giving this vigorous twining climber a strong support to scale, since it can reach 20 to 40 feet. Shirobana is a white-flowered selection of chocolate vine, bearing spicy, chocolate-scented, cream-white flowers in early spring instead of the maroon-purple blooms of the wild species, on the same fast-growing, semi-evergreen to deciduous vine. Like other Akebia quinata selections it fruits best with a second, genetically distinct plant nearby for cross-pollination, though many gardeners grow it for the flowers and foliage alone. Prune hard right after flowering to control its vigorous spread, since chocolate vine can escape into nearby woodland edges in mild climates.
